title: The Law of Total Probability
short: Split into cases A₁, …, Aₙ that cover every outcome without overlapping: P(B) = Σ P(B ∣ Aᵢ) P(Aᵢ).
trouble: Students add the conditional probabilities P(B ∣ Aᵢ) without weighting each one by P(Aᵢ).

blocks.html: Sometimes P(B) is hard to see directly but easy once you know which "case" you are in: which machine made the part, which bag the marble came from. The law of total probability splits a problem into such cases. It is the joint-from-conditional rule, applied once per case, followed by the addition axiom.

If $A_1, \ldots, A_n$ are disjoint and together cover the sample space (a partition), then $$\role[total probability of B]{evidence}{P(B)} = \role[likelihood]{likelihood}{P(B \mid A_1)}\role[prior]{prior}{P(A_1)} + \cdots + \role[likelihood]{likelihood}{P(B \mid A_n)}\role[prior]{prior}{P(A_n)}.$$

$B$ is the disjoint union of the pieces $B \cap A_1, \ldots, B \cap A_n$, because every outcome lies in exactly one $A_i$. By the addition axiom, $P(B) = \sum P(B \cap A_i)$, and each piece is $P(B \cap A_i) = P(B \mid A_i)P(A_i)$. So $P(B)$ is a weighted average of the conditional probabilities, with the case probabilities as weights.

blocks.name: tree
blocks.cap: A probability tree for three machines: multiply along each branch, then add the defective outcomes.

blocks.title: Three machines
blocks.q: Machines A, B and C make 50%, 30% and 20% of a factory's parts, and 1%, 2% and 4% of their parts are defective. Find the probability that a random part is defective.
steps: The machine is the case: the three cases are disjoint and cover every part.
blocks.a: $0.019$, a weighted average of 1%, 2% and 4%, pulled toward machine A's rate because A makes the most parts.

blocks.title: Two bags
blocks.q: Flip a fair coin. Heads: draw from bag I with 3 red and 2 blue marbles. Tails: draw from bag II with 1 red and 4 blue. Find P(red).

blocks.title: The second draw
blocks.q: A box has 5 red and 3 blue marbles. Draw one and set it aside without looking, then draw a second. Find the probability that the second is red.
steps: Condition on the first draw. If it was red (probability $\frac{5}{8}$), 4 of the remaining 7 are red; if blue (probability $\frac{3}{8}$), 5 of 7 are red.
The same as for the first draw. Without seeing the first marble, the second is equally likely to be any of the 8.

blocks.html: The law also runs backward. If the overall defect rate is known and one machine's rate is not, write the weighted sum with that rate as the unknown and solve: with the numbers above, $0.019 = 0.005 + 0.006 + 0.2x$ gives $x = 0.04$.

Adding the conditional probabilities without the weights: $1\% + 2\% + 4\% = 7\%$ is not a probability of anything here, and the plain average $2.33\%$ ignores that machine A makes half the parts. Check: the answer must lie between the smallest and largest conditional probability, nearer the ones with big weights.
